concept: MLX Python scalar weak typing with half-precision arrays
summary: `to_arrays(a, b)` has four cases: two arrays keep their dtypes; an array and a non-array treat the non-array as a weak Python type; the mirror case; and two non-arrays are converted without a target dtype.

facts.text: `to_arrays(a, b)` has four cases: two arrays keep their dtypes; an array and a non-array treat the non-array as a weak Python type; the mirror case; and two non-arrays are converted without a target dtype.
For an array and a scalar it calls `to_array(scalar, array.dtype())`, so the scalar is built with the array's dtype as the requested dtype.

A Python float with a requested floating dtype is cast to C `float` and stored with that dtype. With a half-precision array the result is a float16 or bfloat16 scalar, so the operation stays in half precision.
If the requested dtype is not floating (an integer or bool array) a Python float becomes float32, so int32 array times 0.5 follows normal int32-with-float32 promotion to float32.
A Python int is built as int32 (int64 beyond the int32 range) unless a dtype is requested. With a half-precision array the requested dtype is the half type, so the integer does not promote the array.
For integer target dtypes narrower than 8 bytes the code range-checks the value and throws "Converting N to <dtype> would result in overflow." The float branch has no range check.
The scalar-with-array path in the Python layer ends in the C++ op, where `promote_types` then sees two equal half dtypes and keeps the half type.
Two Python scalars with no array use default types (int32, float32) and are not weak.
PR 2861 earlier fixed `python/src/convert.cpp` so that `mx.array(v, dtype=mx.float64)` casts to double.

2026-08-12: PR 4173 (merged by zcbenz) changed `to_array` to cast a Python float straight to double when the resolved dtype is float64, because `float64_array * 0.1` had used `float32(0.1)`. The PR states that weak promotion is untouched and that nothing changes for float16, bfloat16 or float32. PR 4181, a duplicate, was closed.
The same PR notes `mx.pad` resolves `constant_values` in the input dtype after it, so an out-of-range Python int now raises instead of wrapping.

A large Python float is cast to the half dtype without a range check, so `x_fp16 * 1e5` uses an fp16 scalar of inf. A scalar above 65,504 therefore turns an fp16 operation into inf or NaN, whereas the same scalar against a bf16 array stays finite.
A Python float's digits are rounded to float32 first, then to the half type, so a scalar like 1e-8 against an fp16 array becomes 0 (below fp16's smallest subnormal about 6e-8).
Because the scalar is weak, `x_fp16 * mx.array(0.5)` (a 0-d float32 array) behaves differently from `x_fp16 * 0.5`: the first promotes to float32, the second stays fp16.
Wrapping a constant in `mx.array(...)` or `mx.float32(...)` in model code therefore silently widens activations to float32 and doubles memory traffic; passing the bare Python number does not.
MLX's `to_arrays` treats a non-array operand as a weak Python type when the other operand is an array.
`to_array(scalar, array.dtype())` builds a Python float as the array's floating dtype, so fp16 and bf16 arrays keep their dtype under scalar arithmetic.
A Python float against an integer or bool array becomes float32 because a non-floating requested dtype is replaced by float32.
A Python int is int32, or int64 outside the int32 range, when no dtype is requested.
Integer scalars requested as an integer dtype narrower than 8 bytes raise an overflow error when out of range; the floating-point branch has no such check.
Two Python scalars with no array operand are converted with default types and are not weak.
PR 4173 (merged 2026-08-12) makes `to_array` cast Python floats to double for a float64 target and leaves float16, bfloat16 and float32 behavior unchanged.
PR 4173 states that a Python float still does not promote a float32 array.
PR 4181 duplicated the same fix and was closed as a duplicate.
A Python float larger than 65,504 against an fp16 array becomes inf in the operand, with no warning.
A 0-d float32 `mx.array` operand is not weak and promotes an fp16 array to float32, unlike the bare Python number.
